deck.headline: US proposes tariffs on 14 economies as inflation hits 3.8% and tech stocks swing
deck.sub: India faces up to 25%, Vietnam 35%, the EU 15%; hearings in January, so nothing takes effect this year
deck.summary: The US proposed new tariffs on 14 economies, from 15% for the EU and Japan to 25% for India and 35% for Vietnam, with hearings in January. October PCE inflation hit 3.8%. The Nasdaq 100 briefly entered a bear market before closing down 0.6%.
deck.whyItMatters: Greer calls it a 'top-up' that replaces earlier tariffs, but with inflation near twice the Fed's target a December hike looks more likely; exporters in India and South-East Asia, and the banks financing their trade, have until 5 Jan to make their case.
deck.checked: Checked on the USTR release and BEA's PCE and GDP releases (opened); closing prices from Yahoo Finance data
deck.storyline: Storyline: trade deals around US tariffs · day 3
deck.detailHtml:
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer ruled on 25 Nov that 14 economies' industrial policies create 'structural excess capacity' and are actionable under Section 301, and proposed tariffs on all their goods, net of existing duties and with product exemptions: up to 35% on Vietnam (20% with a trade deal), 25% on India, 20% on China (stacking on existing levies) and Singapore, 18% on Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand, and 15% on the EU, Japan, Korea, Taiwan and Switzerland. Mexico and Norway were not ruled on. Comments are due 5 Jan and hearings start 25 Jan 2027. The same morning BEA reported October PCE inflation at 3.8% (core 3.3%) and revised Q3 growth up to 4.3%.

Markets lurched: the Nasdaq 100 fell nearly 5% intraday and briefly sat 20% below its October record (bear-market territory) before buyers returned. It closed down 0.6%; the S&P 500 lost 0.3% and the Dow gained 0.3%. Nvidia closed 3.9% lower at $149.30. US markets are shut for Thanksgiving and open for a short session on Friday.

The Trump administration has rebuilt its tariff wall on a different legal footing. After the Supreme Court struck down the emergency 'Liberation Day' tariffs in February, USTR opened Section 301 investigations into 16 economies in March. On 25 Nov it ruled against 14 of them and proposed new duties of 15% to 35%, mostly replacing rather than adding to earlier levies (China is the exception). Nothing takes effect before the January hearings.

The timing hurt: the same morning, October PCE inflation came in at 3.8%, nearly double the Fed's 2% goal, and Q3 growth was revised up to 4.3%, strengthening the case for a December rate rise. Tech stocks, already shaken by Nvidia's leadership crisis and doubts about AI spending, swung wildly before closing only modestly lower.

deck.headline: Hackers got into FinCEN, the US anti-money-laundering agency; bank filing deadlines extended
deck.summary: FinCEN, the US Treasury agency that collects banks' suspicious-activity reports, says an intruder accessed some of its systems. It took systems offline, kept the filing site running and gave filers until 30 December for reports due from 18 November. The FBI and CISA are investigating; the scope is unknown.
deck.whyItMatters: FinCEN holds the most sensitive financial intelligence in the US; banks should log which filings were delayed, use the hotline for urgent cases, and assume SAR-related data could be a phishing lure until the scope is known. It is the latest in a string of US government breaches this month.
deck.checked: Checked on CyberScoop, The Register and PYMNTS' quote of the FinCEN order (opened); FinCEN's own notice page did not load
deck.storyline: Storyline: hacks on US government systems · day 2
deck.detailHtml: FinCEN, the US Treasury unit that receives banks' suspicious-activity and currency-transaction reports, says an unauthorised party gained access to 'a limited subset' of its systems. It took some systems offline as a precaution; the BSA E-Filing site stays up but some services may be unavailable. An order gives filers using Secure Data Transfer Mode, and beneficial-ownership filers, until 30 Dec for reports due between 18 Nov and 29 Dec. A source told CyberScoop the FBI, CISA and outside forensics firms are investigating and there is no evidence the beneficial-ownership database was breached. FinCEN has not said how the attacker got in or for how long. The Financial Institutions Hotline still works for urgent tips.

deck.headline: OpenAI, Anthropic and Google post a burst of AI proofs of decades-old problems
deck.summary: OpenAI posted AI-generated proofs claiming matrix multiplication's exponent is exactly 9/4 and that VP differs from VNP; Anthropic posted its own VP proof; Google's Gemini-based Cogentic posted a proven factoring bound. The factoring algorithm is far slower than today's methods, so RSA is not affected. Most results await expert review.
deck.whyItMatters: So what for banks: the factoring result proves a bound of the same family as today's best method, but its constant (105) makes it far slower in practice, so RSA and elliptic-curve keys are not affected. Rumours that a lab can factor in polynomial time are unverified. The pace still argues for keeping post-quantum (and 'post-AI') migration plans on schedule.
deck.checked: Checked on OpenAI's math repository history and Google's Cogentic folder (opened); Anthropic's VP ≠ VNP post seen only via Latent Space and Scott Aaronson; results not yet peer reviewed
deck.detailHtml: OpenAI added nine manuscripts to its public math repository on 24 Nov, produced by an unreleased internal model with selected Lean formalisations. They claim the matrix multiplication exponent ω is exactly 9/4 (a matching lower bound to October's upper bound), that VP and VNP differ (algebraic analogue of P vs NP), near-tight bounds for the Fourier transform and integer multiplication, a strongly polynomial algorithm for linear programming (Smale's ninth problem) and a disproof of the polynomial Hirsch conjecture. Anthropic posted its own VP ≠ VNP proof the same day, Latent Space reports. Google Research's Cogentic agent, running on Gemini 4, posted six papers on 25 Nov with no human help beyond the prompt, including unconditional integer factorisation in time LN[1/3, 105] and faster discrete logarithms in small-characteristic fields. Scott Aaronson calls it 'a whole new continent of mathematical truth'; experts have not yet reviewed most results.

deck.headline: Microsoft, Italy and Switzerland: state hackers now run AI attack tools such as Artex
deck.summary: Microsoft says Chinese state hackers including Salt Typhoon now use Artex, an AI tool that automates intrusions; reports link it to attacks on US intelligence agencies. Italy and Switzerland warn that teams of AI agents are compromising exposed infrastructure systems within hours.
deck.whyItMatters: AI agents shrink the gap between a disclosed flaw and mass exploitation to hours. Shrink internet-facing management interfaces, patch known-exploited bugs first and watch for bursts of parallel probing.
deck.detailHtml: Microsoft says Chinese state-backed groups Salt Typhoon and Crystal Typhoon, North Korean actors and criminal gangs are using Artex, an AI platform released in July that automates several stages of an intrusion, for network reconnaissance, credential attacks, web-app exploitation and hunting exposed secrets in public code. The Record notes the NYT and NextGov reported Artex was allegedly used against the CIA, NGA and ODNI (see yesterday's CIA breach). Separately, CSIRT Italia and Switzerland's cyber agency warn of large campaigns in which several AI agents worked in parallel to compromise many exposed systems in hours, chaining low-severity flaws and writing code on the fly to evade endpoint tools; they name Artex, CyberStrikeAI, a 'DeepSeek Harness' red-team setup (one coordinator, five agents) and PentAGI.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGThe Record: Microsoft says China's Salt Typhoon hackers are using Artex · BleepingComputer: Italy and Switzerland warn of autonomous AI-driven cyberattacks

deck.headline: 1Password: attacker used a staff GitHub account to steal customer names and emails
deck.summary: 1Password says an attacker took over an employee's GitHub account, reached its build systems and pushed code that downloaded some customers' names, emails and account metadata. Password vaults were never exposed and credentials have been rotated, but the data could fuel targeted phishing.
deck.whyItMatters: The stolen data is ideal for convincing phishing aimed at 1Password users, including enterprise admins; warn staff, and treat unexpected 'recover your account' or provisioning emails as hostile.
deck.storyline: Storyline: attacks through software and vendors · day 11
deck.detailHtml: 1Password began investigating on 19 Nov after signs that an attacker had taken over an employee's corporate GitHub account. The attacker read private source code, reached the company's CI/CD system and pushed malicious code to backend services that downloaded account records for a subset of users: names, email addresses, account and user IDs, creation and last sign-in times, public keys, SRP parameters and the tokens in some emailed invitation, provisioning and recovery links. The company says vault contents were 'at no time' accessible, it never holds account passwords or Secret Keys, and it has rotated all possibly exposed credentials. It has not said how many users were affected. The Hacker News thread passed 1,000 points.

deck.headline: Palo Alto patches firewall root-access flaw already exploited alongside PHP2Shell bugs
deck.summary: Palo Alto Networks confirms attackers exploited a Linux kernel flaw called Fragnesia on its firewalls, chaining it with October's PHP2Shell bugs to get root access through exposed management interfaces. Fixes are out for all supported PAN-OS versions; locking down the management interface blocks the attack.
deck.whyItMatters: If any PAN-OS management interface faces the internet, restrict it to internal addresses today and apply both the PHP2Shell and Fragnesia fixes.
deck.storyline: Storyline: critical patches to apply now · day 2
deck.detailHtml: Palo Alto Networks says exploitation of Fragnesia (CVE-2026-46300), a Linux kernel flaw that lets a low-privileged user become root, has been seen against PAN-OS devices whose management interface is exposed to the internet. Attackers chain it with the PHP2Shell bugs (CVE-2026-109618 and -109619) to plant root-level webshells; Palo Alto patched PHP2Shell on 30 Oct and says devices with that fix are protected from this chain. Fixes for Fragnesia now cover PAN-OS 10.2, 11.1, 11.2, 12.1 and 12.2. SecurityWeek says an AI-assisted Chinese-speaking group used the chain in October to compromise 24 firewalls and a management server at a US government-affiliated organisation.

deck.headline: UK household energy bills to jump 26% in January as wholesale gas prices climb
deck.summary: Ofgem says the GB energy price cap rises 26% for a typical household from 1 January, with electricity at 32.69p per kWh and gas at 10.96p, because wholesale gas prices have climbed. Fixed-tariff customers are not affected.
deck.whyItMatters: A quarter-on-quarter jump this size feeds straight into UK inflation and the Bank of England's next decision, and lenders should expect more arrears among stretched borrowers this winter.
deck.detailHtml: Britain's energy regulator Ofgem says prices for a typical household on a default tariff paying by Direct Debit will rise 26% from 1 January to 31 March 2027. Electricity averages 32.69p per kWh with a 54.77p daily standing charge (the government has removed VAT from electricity bills from October 2026 to June 2027); gas averages 10.96p per kWh with a 29.65p standing charge. Ofgem blames higher wholesale gas prices and higher winter use. Fixed-tariff customers are not affected.

deck.headline: FCC lets SpaceX launch up to one million data-centre satellites by 2040
deck.summary: The FCC conditionally approved SpaceX's plan for up to one million Starmind satellites working as data centres in orbit, about 50 times today's satellite count. SpaceX has until 2035 for 100,000 and 2040 for the full constellation; whether space data centres can pay off is unproven.
deck.whyItMatters: The licence turns orbital compute from a pitch into a regulated asset for SpaceX (and any Tesla tie-up), and sets a precedent rivals such as Google and Blue Origin, which plan their own orbital tests, will cite.
deck.storyline: Storyline: data centres in orbit · day 3
deck.detailHtml: The FCC granted SpaceX conditional authorisation for up to 1 million Starmind satellites meant to work as orbital data centres, about 50 times the number of satellites in orbit today. Chairman Brendan Carr called it 'a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure'. Ars Technica notes the order gives SpaceX seven years to deploy its first operational Starmind satellite, until November 2035 for 100,000 and November 2040 for the full constellation, and does not establish that space data centres are technically or economically viable. Astronomers and space-debris experts are sceptical.

deck.headline: FDA approves Neuralink's pivotal brain-implant trial, the first in the US
deck.summary: Neuralink says the FDA approved its LINK Pivotal Study, the first US pivotal trial of an implanted brain-computer interface, and is recruiting now; reports say it is for people with ALS. A pivotal trial is the last step before seeking market approval.
deck.whyItMatters: Brain implants move from experiments toward a regulated medical product, raising near-term questions for insurers on coverage and pricing.
deck.storyline: Storyline: brain implants reaching patients · day 1
deck.detailHtml: Neuralink says the FDA has approved its LINK Pivotal Study, which it calls the first pivotal trial for an implantable brain-computer interface in the US, and that recruitment is open. Bloomberg and MobiHealthNews report the trial is for people with ALS. A pivotal study is the stage that produces the evidence for market approval. Neuralink's earlier feasibility work included a VOICE study restoring speech in ALS patients and a self-supervised decoder that set an 11.32 bits-per-second record.

deck.headline: BNY and Microsoft let AI agents negotiate a Treasury bill trade within set limits
deck.summary: BNY and Microsoft ran a pilot where AI agents on both sides negotiated a US Treasury bill trade within preset limits, with every message, control check and human decision recorded under BNY's new protocol. BNY plans to extend it to repo deals.
deck.whyItMatters: An audit trail designed for agent-to-agent negotiation is the piece regulators will ask for; trading and treasury teams should watch whether the protocol becomes an industry standard.
deck.storyline: Storyline: AI agents and financial firms · day 9
deck.detailHtml: BNY, which has $63.4 trillion under custody or administration, completed a pilot with Microsoft in which AI agents on both sides of a US Treasury bill trade negotiated the price within predefined limits. BNY's patent-pending Agentic Negotiation Protocol records the messages exchanged, control checks and human decisions. BNY plans to extend it to repurchase agreements and multiparty negotiations. PYMNTS Intelligence finds only 32% of CFOs highly interested in treasury agents and 47% would give them no access.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGPYMNTS: BNY and Microsoft let AI agents haggle over Treasurys

deck.headline: Japan's SMFG and SBI launch a Solana venture for stablecoins and tokenised assets
deck.summary: SBI Holdings and megabank SMFG launched SBI Solana Global with the Solana Foundation to build stablecoin payments, tokenise financial and real-world assets and explore micropayments for AI agents across Asia. It is one of the largest banks yet to back a public-blockchain venture.
deck.whyItMatters: A megabank putting its name on a public-blockchain venture is a signal to Asian banks weighing permissioned versus public chains for tokenised deposits and stablecoins.
deck.detailHtml: SBI Holdings and Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group (SMFG), one of Japan's three megabanks, finalised a joint venture with the Solana Foundation, converting SBI R3 Japan into SBI Solana Global, which has begun full operations. It will work on stablecoin payment infrastructure, tokenisation of financial and real-world assets, onchain asset management and micropayments for AI agents across Asia. Thirteen outlets covered it.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGCointelegraph: Japan's SBI, SMFG launch Solana venture for stablecoins, tokenization

deck.headline: 42 US states move to block bankrupt Character.AI from auctioning users' private chats
deck.summary: Forty-two US state attorneys general are trying to stop bankrupt Character.AI from selling chat histories from over 21 million US accounts, including 2.1 million minors. The only named bidder is a Delaware company formed on 13 November.
deck.whyItMatters: AI conversation logs are becoming saleable assets in insolvency; any firm whose staff or customers use chatbots should check what happens to that data if the vendor fails.
deck.storyline: Storyline: privacy fines on big tech · day 3
deck.detailHtml: A coalition of 42 state attorneys general has intervened in Character.AI's Chapter 11 case (filed in October) to stop the company selling user data. They say the dataset holds chat histories from more than 21 million US accounts, over 2.1 million belonging to minors, plus IP addresses, and that Character.AI had told users their personal information would not be sold. The only disclosed bidder is Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC, a Delaware company formed on 13 Nov. Character.AI says users' information stays protected by its privacy policy.

deck.headline: Australia passes law making big tech prevent foreseeable online harms or face big fines
deck.summary: Australia passed a Digital Duty of Care Act that requires platforms to detect and reduce foreseeable online harms before they happen, with possible fines in the billions. Australia's earlier under-16 social media ban has been copied worldwide.
deck.whyItMatters: A 'duty of care' standard shifts the test from removing bad content to proving you anticipated it; expect AI chatbots and agents to fall within scope and other governments to copy it.
deck.storyline: Storyline: laws making platforms prevent harm · day 1
deck.detailHtml: Australia's Parliament passed the Digital Duty of Care Act on 25 Nov with strong backing from Prime Minister Anthony Albanese. It requires online providers to set up protocols to detect and reduce risks from harmful content before harm occurs, including threats of violence and rape, and opens the way to fines in the billions of dollars. Australia's under-16 social media ban, in force since December 2025, has been copied worldwide.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGThe Record: Australia passes tough legislation requiring big tech to preempt foreseeable harms

deck.headline: Nvidia slides again and settles old crypto-revenue suit for $290m
deck.summary: Nvidia fell another 3.9% to $149.30 as the rally after Jensen Huang's return faded. It agreed to pay $290 million to settle a 2018 lawsuit over crypto-mining revenue disclosures, denying wrongdoing. Huang told staff he is in therapy; he faces House questions on 1 December.
deck.whyItMatters: The settlement closes an old legal overhang, but the stock now trades on governance headlines, which matters for the many AI firms Nvidia supplies and finances.
deck.update: Shares fall 3.9% more to $149.30; Nvidia agrees a $290m settlement of the 2018 crypto-mining disclosure suit
deck.detailHtml: Nvidia closed 3.9% lower at $149.30 on Wednesday, after falling as much as 8.7% intraday, as Monday's reinstatement rally kept fading. A court filing shows Nvidia agreed to pay $290m in cash to settle a 2018 class action alleging it misled investors about how much gaming revenue came from crypto miners in 2017-18; it denies wrongdoing, and the sum is about 14% of the $2.06bn the plaintiffs' expert estimated. Huang apologised and told staff at an all-hands meeting he is in therapy, the WSJ and The Information report. He faces House committee questions on 1 Dec.

alsoToday.headline: Taiwan's central bank would make stablecoin issuers park 10.775% of reserves with it
alsoToday.summary: The Central Bank of the Republic of China (Taiwan) published draft regulations on 25 Nov under which issuers of stablecoins denominated in Taiwan dollars or foreign currencies would deposit 10.775% of their backing assets in an account at the central bank, the same as an existing bank reserve ratio, Central Banking reports.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Treating stablecoin reserves like bank deposits narrows the gap between issuers and banks, and makes Taiwan-dollar coins less profitable for non-banks.

alsoToday.headline: Ukraine legalises crypto trading and taxes gains at 23% from July 2027
alsoToday.summary: Ukraine's Verkhovna Rada passed bill No. 10225-d with 271 votes, legalising the crypto market from 1 July 2027. Profits are taxed at 18% plus a 5% military levy; swaps between crypto assets are not taxed.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: One of Europe's biggest retail crypto markets moves into the regulated system, with the central bank, not a markets regulator, holding the stablecoin keys.
alsoToday.storyline: Storyline: who runs US crypto regulation · day 5
alsoToday.detailHtml: Ukraine's Verkhovna Rada passed bill No. 10225-d with 271 votes, legalising the crypto market from 1 July 2027. Profits are taxed at 18% plus a 5% military levy; swaps between crypto assets are not taxed. The National Bank of Ukraine will oversee stablecoins and exchanges that convert crypto to cash and can allow or ban stablecoin circulation. Lawmakers expect about 15bn hryvnias ($330m) of extra revenue. President Zelensky still has to sign it.

alsoToday.whyItMatters: A multi-day outage at a top-five US insurer during holiday travel is the kind of operational-resilience failure supervisors now test for; no sign yet of a cyberattack.

alsoToday.headline: ESA's Hera finds NASA's DART left a stadium-sized crater on asteroid Dimorphos
alsoToday.summary: ESA's Hera spacecraft has sent the first close images of Dimorphos, the asteroid NASA's DART probe deliberately hit in 2022 to test whether a space rock can be pushed off course. They show a stadium-sized crater; 'the crater is almost as large as the body itself', said Hera scientist Sabina Raducan.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Real crater data lets scientists model how much a kinetic impactor can deflect a threatening asteroid.

alsoToday.headline: Unconfirmed: a rival says Jev, TypeSafe's decision-only model, is built on Qwen
alsoToday.summary: Modaic says tests of self-identification, tokenizer behaviour and throughput point to Jev, TypeSafe AI's decision-only 'System One' model, being built on Alibaba's open Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. TypeSafe does not disclose Jev's base model and has not responded.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Unverified; if true it matters for licensing and supplier-risk reviews of anyone deploying Jev.
alsoToday.storyline: Storyline: new kinds of AI models · day 13
alsoToday.detailHtml: Modaic says tests of self-identification, tokenizer behaviour and throughput point to Jev, TypeSafe AI's decision-only 'System One' model, being built on Alibaba's open Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. TypeSafe does not disclose Jev's base model and has not responded. Hacker News commenters note Modaic is a TypeSafe competitor and that building on an open base model would not by itself undo Jev's novelty, which lies in answering with a decision instead of generated text.
